title: Franz Schubert
wiki_lead:
Franz Peter Schubert (; German: [fʁants ˈpeːtɐ ˈʃuːbɐt]; 31 January 1797 – 19 November 1828) was an Austrian composer of the late Classical and early Romantic eras. He was immensely prolific despite living a short life, leaving behind a vast oeuvre of more than 1,000 compositions, including over 600 Lieder (art song in German) and other vocal works, seven complete symphonies, sacred music, operas, incidental music, and a large body of piano and chamber music. Among these are the songs "Gretchen am Spinnrade", "Erlkönig" and "Ave Maria"; the Trout Quintet; the Symphony in B minor, "Unfinished"; the Symphony in C major, "The Great"; the String Quartet No. 14 in D minor (Death and the Maiden); the String Quintet in C major; the Impromptus for solo piano; the last three piano sonatas; the Fantasia in F minor for piano four hands; the incidental music to the play Rosamunde; the song cycles Die schöne Müllerin and Winterreise; and the song collection Schwanengesang.
Born in the Himmelpfortgrund suburb of Vienna, Schubert showed uncommon gifts for music from an early age. His father gave him his first violin lessons and his elder brother gave him piano lessons, but Schubert soon surpassed their abilities. In 1808, at the age of eleven, he became a pupil at the Stadtkonvikt school, where he became acquainted with the orchestral music of Joseph Haydn, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, and Ludwig van Beethoven. He left the Stadtkonvikt at the end of 1813 and returned home to live with his father, where he began studying to become a schoolteacher. Despite this, he continued his studies in composition with Antonio Salieri and still composed prolifically. In 1821, Schubert was admitted to the Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde as a performing member, which helped establish his name among the Viennese citizenry. He gave a concert of his works to critical acclaim in March 1828, the only time he did so in his career. He died eight months later at the age of 31, the cause officially attributed to typhoid fever, but believed by some historians to be syphilis.
Appreciation of Schubert's music while he was alive was limited to a relatively small circle of admirers in Vienna, but interest in his work increased greatly in the decades following his death. Felix Mendelssohn, Robert Schumann, Franz Liszt, Johannes Brahms and other 19th-century composers discovered and championed his works. Today, Schubert is considered one of the greatest composers in the history of Western classical music and his music continues to be widely performed.

Life and career


Early life and education

Franz Peter Schubert was born in Himmelpfortgrund (now a part of Alsergrund), Vienna, Archduchy of Austria, on 31 January 1797, and baptized in the Catholic Church the following day. He was the twelfth child of Franz Theodor Florian Schubert (1763–1830) and Maria Elisabeth Katharina Vietz (1756–1812). Schubert's immediate ancestors came originally from the province of Zuckmantel in Austrian Silesia. His father, the son of a Moravian peasant, was a well-known parish schoolmaster, and his school in Lichtental (in Vienna's ninth district) had numerous students in attendance. He came to Vienna from Zuckmantel in 1784 and was appointed schoolmaster two years later. His mother was the daughter of a Silesian master locksmith and had been a housemaid for a Viennese family before marriage. Of Franz Theodor and Elisabeth's fourteen children (one of them illegitimate, born in 1783), only five survived to adulthood.
At the age of five, Schubert began to receive regular lessons from his father, and a year later he was enrolled at his father's school. Although it is not known exactly when he received his first musical instruction, he was given piano lessons by his brother Ignaz, but they lasted for a very short time as Schubert exceeded him within a few months. grok_lead: Franz Schubert (1797â1828) was an Austrian composer of the late Classical and early Romantic eras, best known for his extraordinary melodic gift and prolific output of over 1,500 works, including more than 600 lieder (art songs), symphonies, chamber music, and piano pieces, all composed within his brief 31-year lifespan. Born on January 31, 1797, in Vienna to a schoolteacher father who taught him the violin and viola, his elder brother Ignaz who provided early piano lessons, and Michael Holzer, the organist and choirmaster at the Lichtental parish church, who provided singing instruction, Schubert displayed prodigious talent from childhood, with his earliest surviving compositions dating from 1810 when he was 13, and studying counterpoint under Antonio Salieri after joining the Imperial Chapel choir in 1808. He left the Stadtkonvikt around 1813 after his voice broke and, following teacher training, served as an assistant teacher at his father's school from 1814 until around 1818. By his late teens, he had already produced several hundred works, including groundbreaking lieder such as Gretchen am Spinnrade (1814) and ErlkÃ¶nig (1815), which established him as an innovator in the art song form by blending vocal melody with evocative piano accompaniment inspired by Goethe's poetry. Schubert's career, though marked by financial hardship and limited public recognition during his lifetime, saw him quit teaching around 1818 to focus on composition, producing masterpieces like the Unfinished Symphony (commonly No. 8, or No. 7 in the Neue Schubert-Ausgabe, 1822), the Great C Major Symphony (commonly No. 9, or No. 8 in the Neue Schubert-Ausgabe, 1826), the Trout Quintet (1819), and song cycles such as Die SchÃ¶ne MÃ¼llerin (1823) and Die Winterreise (1827), which explored themes of longing, nature, and mortality with profound emotional depth. Influenced by Haydn, Mozart, and Beethovenâwhose praises he earned despite never meeting himâSchubert bridged the Classical restraint of his predecessors with the Romantic emphasis on personal expression and harmonic innovation, often performing his own works in intimate Viennese gatherings. His health declined after contracting syphilis in early 1823, which he first confessed to his close friend Franz von Schober on February 28, 1823, leading to increasing isolation, yet he continued composing prolifically until his death from typhoid fever, possibly due to complications from syphilis, on November 19, 1828; buried initially in Vienna's WÃ¤hring cemetery near Beethoven, his remains were later moved to the Zentralfriedhof. Schubert's legacy, fully realized posthumously through publications by admirers such as Franz Liszt and Robert Schumann, cemented his status as a cornerstone of Western classical music, influencing generations of composers including Mendelssohn, Brahms, and Mahler with his lyrical intimacy and structural ingenuity.
